action_criteria.expected_evidence: Hoover sign in both legs with preserved reflexes, flexor plantars and no sensory level
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: Acute paraplegia with a bilateral Hoover sign, normal reflexes and intact sensation is diagnosed at the bedside: the Hoover sign shows clinical incompatibility (DSM-5 criterion B; McWhirter 2011; Daum 2014).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cord caliber and signal from the cervical cord to the conus, with no compression
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI, once
action_criteria.rationale: Acute paraplegia is treated as a possible cord emergency (compression or myelitis); even with positive signs and a normal sensory and sphincter examination, one spine MRI is the specific question imaging answers here (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No parasagittal or other brain lesion
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast brain MRI
action_criteria.rationale: A parasagittal lesion can cause paraparesis, but with a bilateral Hoover sign and normal reflexes a brain scan answers no specific question; one scan is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of the comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: Low mood and distress after the exam failure are a treatment target; a battery can quantify them but does not make the diagnosis (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive signs and treatment trials in FND
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis and the plan rest on this patient's examination and recorded data, not on a search.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional limb weakness of both legs) based on the bilateral Hoover sign with preserved reflexes, flexor plantars, intact sensation and normal sphincter function, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid low mood and distress since the exam failure, after screening for depression.

avoided_actions.rationale: There are no events, palpitations or syncope; the mild tachycardia of a distressed patient raises no cardiac question.
No murmur, embolic or structural cardiac question in a healthy 22-year-old with functional paraplegia.
There are no episodes of any kind; rhythm monitoring answers no question.
A head CT does not answer the cord question of acute paraplegia; the spine MRI does.
PET has no role in functional weakness.
Reflexes are preserved and the bilateral Hoover sign shows normal involuntary power; nerve conduction studies and EMG answer no question and a normal study reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Sensation is intact with no sensory level; evoked potentials have no question to answer.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — bilateral functional leg weakness (paraplegia)

differential.key_features: Acute paraplegia raises compression, but there is no back pain, no sensory level and no sphincter disturbance, reflexes are preserved with flexor plantars, the Hoover sign is positive on both sides and the spine MRI shows no compression.

differential.diagnosis: Acute transverse myelitis (including NMOSD or MOGAD myelitis)
differential.key_features: A myelitis severe enough to cause paraplegia is expected to give a sensory level and bladder involvement; sensation and sphincters are normal and the spine MRI shows normal cord signal and caliber.
Acute bilateral leg weakness raises GBS, but there is no preceding illness, no sensory symptoms or pain, reflexes are preserved and the Hoover sign shows normal involuntary hip extension.

Waking with weakness after rest raises a periodic paralysis, but reflexes are preserved, involuntary hip extension is full on Hoover testing and she walks normally when unobserved, none of which fits a paralytic attack.

key_clinical_evidence: Bilateral Hoover sign: full involuntary hip extension in each leg during attempted flexion of the other, against 0/5 and 1/5 voluntary power.
Preserved symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, intact sensation with no level and normal bladder and bowel function 24 hours into a complete paraplegia are incompatible with an acute cord lesion.
She walks independently to the bathroom when unaware of being observed: supportive inconsistency, not a rule-in sign.
One spine MRI, indicated by acute paraplegia, shows a normal cord without compression or signal change.
The exam failure, family pressure, poor sleep and crying are context and a treatment target; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A stressor is supportive context only; the bilateral Hoover sign with a normal reflex, sensory and sphincter examination makes the diagnosis, and acute paraplegia still earns one spine MRI.
red_herrings.data_point: First exam failure 2 weeks ago with strong family pressure, poor sleep and crying
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concluding that stress 'caused' the paraplegia and skipping the examination and the cord imaging

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Abrupt onset is common in functional weakness; the examination and one normal spine MRI answer the cord question.
red_herrings.data_point: Woke unable to move both legs, with abrupt onset overnight
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treating the abrupt onset as proof of a vascular or compressive cord lesion and escalating to repeated or invasive testing

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.finding: Normal caliber and signal; no compression.
Normal caliber and signal; conus terminates at L1; no compression.
Normal alignment and marrow signal; no disc protrusion, epidural collection or canal stenosis.

body_imaging.impression: Normal non-contrast MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine to the conus. No cord compression and no intramedullary signal abnormality.

findings.result: Each hip extends with full strength during attempted flexion of the other hip against resistance, although voluntary hip extension is 0/5 on the right and 1/5 on the left.
Walks independently to the bathroom when unaware of being observed; not counted as a rule-in sign.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric with flexor plantar responses; sensation intact with no sensory level; no bladder or bowel symptoms.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive sign of functional weakness: bilateral Hoover sign. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Review and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder from motor signs of high specificity, and physiotherapy whose effect on the trial's primary outcome was modest; a later revision of the diagnosis is uncommon.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Acute complete paraplegia with a bilateral Hoover sign and a normal reflex, sensory and sphincter examination; the only specific question for imaging is the cord, answered by one spine MRI. Brain imaging, nerve studies and evoked potentials are overuse.
metadata.notes: Straightforward FND: acute bilateral functional leg weakness in a 22-year-old student; bilateral Hoover sign; one spine MRI answers the cord question.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden bilateral leg weakness — unable to walk for 24 hours

social_history.recent_stressor: Major academic exam failure 2 weeks prior; first time failing an exam in her academic career; significant performance pressure from family

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. T is a 22-year-old college senior and pre-medical student who presents with 24 hours of bilateral leg weakness severe enough to prevent ambulation. She reports waking yesterday morning unable to move her legs. She had gone to sleep feeling well after a long study session. She has been a high-achieving student throughout her academic career; however, she failed a major organic chemistry examination 2 weeks ago for the first time, creating significant distress. Her family, who immigrated from West Africa, has invested substantially in her education and she feels immense pressure to succeed and become a physician. She has no prior neurological symptoms. She denies any sensory changes, pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, fever, or headache. She has not had any recent illness. There is no history of trauma. She has no medications and no substance use. Her roommate reports she has been sleeping poorly and crying frequently since the exam failure. The weakness onset was abrupt, occurring overnight without any prodromal symptoms. She denies any prior similar episodes. She has no family history of neurological disease.

neurological_exam.additional: No la belle indifference: she is distressed and appropriately upset.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No facial droop. Gaze intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Non-ambulatory in room; mobilizes independently to bathroom when not aware of observation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Appropriately upset. Insight limited regarding psychological contributors.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral leg weakness: right 0/5, left 1/5 on voluntary testing. Hoover sign positive bilaterally: with the examiner's hands under both heels, attempted flexion of the right hip brings the left heel down with full force, and attempted flexion of the left hip brings the right heel down with full force. Arms 5/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Normal 2+ symmetric. No Babinski or Hoffman.
